questions.q: What does the term 'idiolect' mean?
options: The distinctive speech style of an individual person
The most prestigious accent in a country
The written register of a formal document
questions.explain: An idiolect is the unique combination of vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation used by one individual.

questions.q: What does 'dialect' refer to?
options: The distinctive grammar and vocabulary of a regional or social group
The pronunciation of an individual only
The volume and pace of speech
questions.explain: Dialect covers the characteristic grammar and vocabulary of a regional or social variety, not just pronunciation.

questions.q: What does 'accent' specifically describe?
options: The words a person chooses to use
The structure of a person's sentences
The pattern of turn-taking in talk
questions.explain: Accent refers only to pronunciation, whereas dialect also involves vocabulary and grammar.

questions.q: Which statement best describes Received Pronunciation (RP)?
options: A prestige accent traditionally associated with education and not tied to one region
A regional dialect of northern England
questions.explain: RP is a high-prestige accent historically linked with education and broadcasting and not confined to any single region.

questions.q: What is a 'sociolect'?
options: A variety of language associated with a particular social group
The formal register of written texts
questions.explain: A sociolect is a language variety shared by members of a particular social group.

questions.q: Which is the best description of 'Standard English'?
options: The variety of English widely accepted as the norm in formal and written communication
The accent used only by the royal family
A regional dialect of the south-east
questions.explain: Standard English is the variety accepted as the norm in education, formal and written contexts, and is independent of accent.

questions.q: Which of these are 'non-fluency features' of spoken language?
options: Fillers, hesitations, false starts and repetitions
questions.explain: Non-fluency features are the natural interruptions to smooth speech, such as fillers, hesitations, false starts and repetition.

questions.q: Sounds such as 'um' and 'er' in conversation are examples of what?
questions.explain: 'Um' and 'er' are fillers or voiced pauses that speakers use while planning what to say next.

questions.q: What is the main function of a tag question such as 'It's cold, isn't it?'
options: To invite a response or seek agreement from the listener
questions.explain: A tag question turns a statement into an invitation for the listener to respond or agree.

questions.q: What do 'prosodic features' refer to?
options: Stress, intonation, pitch, rhythm and pace of speech
questions.explain: Prosodic features are the sound qualities of speech such as stress, intonation, pitch, rhythm and pace.

questions.q: What are 'paralinguistic features'?
options: Non-verbal features such as gesture, facial expression and body language
questions.explain: Paralinguistic features are non-verbal aspects of communication, such as gesture, facial expression and body language.

questions.q: What is 'phatic talk' used for?
options: To establish or maintain social relationships rather than convey information
questions.explain: Phatic talk, such as small talk about the weather, maintains social bonds rather than exchanging information.

questions.q: What does 'register' refer to in the study of language?
options: The level of formality and style chosen to suit a particular context
The speed at which a person speaks
questions.explain: Register is the variation in formality and style that speakers adopt to suit the context, purpose and audience.

questions.q: Turn-taking and adjacency pairs are features that reveal information about what?
options: The structure of conversation and spoken interaction
The comparison of two written texts
questions.explain: Turn-taking and adjacency pairs are patterns that show how conversation is structured and managed between speakers.

questions.q: A student records friends chatting and notes frequent slang and overlapping speech. This is best analysed as an investigation of what?
options: Informal spoken language and register within a peer group
The layout of a newspaper article
The rhyme scheme of a poem
questions.explain: Slang and overlaps among friends are features of informal spoken language and the register of a peer group.

questions.q: To compare how a politician speaks in a one-to-one interview and at a large rally, a student should focus on how spoken language changes with what?
questions.explain: Differences between the interview and rally are driven by changes in purpose, audience and context.

questions.q: When analysing written language, what does the term 'form' refer to?
options: The type or genre of the text, such as a letter, article or leaflet
The cost of printing the text
questions.explain: Form is the kind of text or genre, such as a letter, article or leaflet, which shapes its conventions.

questions.q: Identifying devices such as direct address and rhetorical questions helps a student analyse what?
options: How the writer seeks to influence or engage the reader
The number of pages in the text
questions.explain: Rhetorical devices are analysed to show how a writer aims to influence, persuade or engage the reader.

questions.q: When comparing two written texts, an effective response should do what?
options: Examine similarities and differences in purpose, audience, language and structure
Count the words in each text
questions.explain: A strong comparison analyses similarities and differences in purpose, audience, language and structure across both texts.

questions.q: A student compares a charity leaflet and a news report on the same issue. The strongest comparison focuses on what?
options: How each text's language and structure suit its different purpose and audience
Which text uses a larger font
questions.explain: The most analytical comparison links each text's language and structure to its distinct purpose and audience.
